title: Reliable Webhook Delivery and Verification
lesson:
A webhook is an HTTP callback: when an event happens in your system, you POST it to a URL the customer registered. It is simple for consumers but hard for providers, because you are calling servers you do not control, which can be slow, down, or hostile. Treat delivery as an asynchronous job pipeline: write the event to a durable store or queue in the same transaction as the state change (the outbox pattern), and have separate workers do the HTTP calls so a slow consumer never blocks your core request path.

Delivery is at-least-once. Workers should use a short timeout, treat 2xx as success, and retry anything else with exponential backoff and jitter over hours or days. After a long run of failures, stop retrying, mark the endpoint as failing, notify the owner, and let them replay missed events. Because retries and timeouts can cause duplicates, and ordering is not guaranteed across retries, each event should carry a unique event ID so consumers can deduplicate, and consumers should be idempotent.

Consumers must be able to trust where a request came from. The standard approach is signing: the provider computes an HMAC of the raw request body (often with a timestamp) using a per-endpoint shared secret and sends it in a header. The receiver recomputes the HMAC over the raw bytes, compares with a constant-time comparison, and rejects stale timestamps to limit replay attacks. Parsing and re-serializing the JSON before verifying will break the signature.

On the receiving side, the best practice is to verify, persist the event, return 2xx quickly, and process asynchronously. Doing heavy work inline risks timeouts, which make the provider retry and create duplicate work. Providers should also guard against SSRF by refusing to deliver to internal or private IP ranges.

questions.prompt: Why should webhook deliveries be made by background workers rather than inline in the request that caused the event?
options: HTTP calls cannot be made inside request handlers
A slow or down consumer would otherwise block or fail your core request path
Webhooks must be sent in batches only
questions.explanation: Decoupling delivery isolates your core path from consumers you do not control.

questions.prompt: Webhook delivery with retries is typically at-least-once, so consumers should expect duplicate events.
questions.explanation: Timeouts and retries mean an event may be delivered more than once, so consumers deduplicate by event ID.

questions.prompt: Providers typically sign webhook payloads with an ____ computed over the raw body using a shared secret.
questions.explanation: An HMAC lets the receiver verify both the sender's identity and that the body was not altered.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a well-behaved webhook receiver.
items: Verify the signature on the raw body
questions.explanation: Verify first, store durably, acknowledge fast, then do heavy work out of band.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of including a timestamp in the signed payload?
options: To let receivers reject old, replayed requests
questions.explanation: A signed timestamp lets receivers reject captured requests replayed after a tolerance window.
